nameStory: The Golden Sweat Bee gets its name from its stunning metallic golden-green body that shimmers like jewelry in sunlight. Like other sweat bees, it's called a 'sweat bee' because it's attracted to the salt in human perspiration on hot summer days. Don't worry though - these gentle bees rarely sting and are just looking for a mineral snack!
description: The Golden Sweat Bee is a small, brilliantly colored native bee that looks like a tiny flying emerald with golden highlights. These quarter-inch-long pollinators have metallic green bodies that can shimmer with copper, red, or yellow tones depending on how the light hits them. Unlike honeybees, they're solitary nesters that dig small burrows in the ground. They're important pollinators for wildflowers and garden plants throughout New England.

idTips.label: Metallic coloration
idTips.description: Body has a brilliant metallic green sheen that shifts to golden, copper, or reddish tones as it moves in the light - like looking at an oil slick or soap bubble

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Small and compact, about the size of your pinky nail, with a robust build rather than the elongated shape of larger bees

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting flight with frequent hovering near flowers and potential nesting sites, less steady than a honeybee's flight

idTips.label: Behavior around humans
idTips.description: May land gently on sweaty skin or clothing to collect salt - feels like a tiny tickle and shows no aggressive behavior

idTips.label: Head and antennae
idTips.description: Proportionally large head for body size with thin, dark antennae that are constantly moving as they investigate flowers

habitat: Golden Sweat Bees thrive in sunny, open areas with sandy or loose soil perfect for their ground-nesting lifestyle. Look for them in gardens, meadows, forest edges, and even urban parks where wildflowers and cultivated plants provide nectar sources. They prefer areas with a mix of bare ground for nesting and diverse flowering plants within flying distance.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from underground nests and begin establishing new colonies. Look for them visiting early spring flowers like dandelions and fruit tree blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible visiting flowers and may land on sweaty gardeners. This is the best time to observe their brilliant metallic coloration in bright sunlight.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall as they visit late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod. New queens mate and prepare for winter by finding protected spots to hibernate.
seasonality.winter: Dormant underground or in protected crevices. No bee activity visible, but their small ground nests may be detectable as tiny holes in bare soil.

funFact: Golden Sweat Bees are attracted to the same minerals found in sports drinks - when they land on your sweaty arm during gardening, they're essentially getting their version of Gatorade to replenish essential salts and electrolytes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other metallic green sweat bees, but Golden Sweat Bees have that distinctive golden or coppery sheen mixed with the green. Remember: if it looks like a tiny green jewel with golden highlights hovering around your garden, you've found your Golden Sweat Bee!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sweat bees,' these insects are actually beneficial pollinators that rarely sting humans. The family name 'sweat bee' can make people unnecessarily worried, but they're among the gentlest bees you'll encounter in your garden.
compareHints: Golden Sweat Bees are the only Augochlorella species found in New England, making them unique in their genus here. Compared to other metallic sweat bees in the region, they're distinguished by their golden-copper highlights mixed with green, while most other metallic sweat bees are purely green or blue-green. They're also slightly more robust in build than many of their purely green relatives.
